Why AI Struggles To Reuse Chip Designs

50

Shares

6

6

17

AI can accelerate derivative designs, but physical constraints and incomplete data limit how much can be automated.

November 24th, 2026 -

By: Liz Allan

Key Takeaways:

AI can accelerate derivative chip design, but those derivatives may not be physically viable or cost-effective.
AI-assisted reuse depends on the availability of accurate design data, engineering knowledge, and proven methodologies.
End-to-end automation is limited by gaps in multi-physics simulation, implementation, and verification.

Chipmakers are seeing mixed results when they apply AI to derivative and new chip designs, finding that AI-generated solutions can be substantially different and more costly than expected, and that AI-driven designs introduce new manufacturing and verification challenges.
Several key problems have emerged when incorporating AI in chip design. Among them:

The data needed to ensure that follow-on designs will function as expected may not be complete because some of that data resides in other companies, such as foundries, OSATs, and various equipment and process providers;
Integrating rapidly evolving AI capabilities into established EDA flows remains challenging, especially where predictability, traceability, and silicon-proven results are required.
Many organizations have customized tools for their own chips, markets, and expertise, and AI tools have not yet adapted to those changes.

“There’s the engineer in me that says if AI can take us to brave new worlds where humans haven’t yet gone, that’s an exciting thing,” said Nilesh Kamdar, general manager of Keysight EDA. “But I’ve seen it run into problems. For example, I had a low-pass filter, which we call a pixelated model, and it looks like a QR code in the middle. There’s a high-frequency part running at about 2 GHz. If I want to change it to 2.5 GHz, a human would look it up in a textbook. There are traditional ways to do it, and they would create something that any other human would recognize. AI looks at this, says, ‘I don’t understand your textbook, so I’m going to just turn on and off any single part of this grid, and I’ll come up with something.’ It does sort of work, but there are constraints. Is this manufacturable? Is this cost-effective? Did I learn anything out of this? Yes, AI solved a problem for me, but as a human, I had intuition about what worked at 2 GHz. Now, if I want to shift to 2.5 GHz, that same intuition will change the design.”
Instead of making an incremental change to account for a new spec, AI may come up with something completely different, with no correlation between versions, Kamdar explained. “There’s a cost of letting AI do all of these things.”
Reusing designs across multiple generations of chips has long been the go-to strategy as a way of amortizing non-recurring engineering (NRE) costs and reducing development time. Using AI agents to come up with derivatives adds a whole different way of looking at the problem. AI agents can assess existing architectures and RTL to identify potential bottlenecks, explore design modifications, optimize EDA tool settings, and automate portions of verification and debugging. And they can orchestrate workflows across multiple tools, reducing the manual effort required to adapt existing IP to new specifications.
But the resulting AI-generated design is not necessarily ready to be implemented in a follow-on chip. Engineers must determine whether proposed changes are physically feasible, manufacturable, cost-effective, and compatible with the new design’s requirements. That, in turn, will determine where AI can and cannot be used, and where EDA tools need to evolve in order to close that gap.
Software reuse easier than hardware reuse
Despite AI’s promise, a lot of human effort is still needed in today’s designs. Working with natural language interfaces is a big plus, but minor differences in queries can result in very different answers.
“We were rapidly adapting the automotive solution to robotics because there’s a lot of commonality,” said Baaziz Achour, CTO of Qualcomm. [1] “Many of the key functions are similar, such as perception, path planning, and foundational technologies like sensor fusion, object recognition, location, and control. We were able to take the full automotive solution and apply it to robotics. We have very effective solutions for scaling the software. However, hardware IP scaling and SoC integration still require significant human effort.”
Those differences can also be significant across domains. for example, developers may increase the number of cores in an NPU and use tools to analyze bottlenecks as application workloads shift. But this type of scaling is very different with mobile multimedia, such as a camera, Achour explained. “Across a lot of this AI spectrum of products, the basic camera and display blocks are similar, but the requirements are very different in camera count, speed, and power.”

Fig. 1: Designers can use tools to adapt common IP, but there is still a non-recurring engineering cost for SoC implementation. Source: Qualcomm/DAC
While designers can leverage core IP blocks, such as an image signal processor, every processing core, camera, and display across these devices must meet diverse requirements and cost targets. “Currently, we often create separate architectures and hardware design variants for each case,” said Achour. “Can EDA help us build one flexible architecture that adapts to these diverse requirements instead of manually customizing for each time?”
The answer? Maybe. Ensuring that a chip design will function flawlessly requires an ecosystem. Automating some steps in the design flow can help, but how much automation and which steps are still being explored. Nevertheless, there are plenty of places where engineers would welcome more flexibility and automation, such as iteratively tuning EDA tools to meet design targets.
“Three months were spent in recipe tuning of EDA tools,” said Achour. “Neither the RTL nor the floorplan were changed in these iterations, so this is a huge source of inefficiency. EDA tool companies have AI-aided fine-tuning, but that consumes a lot of compute. Further innovation is needed for this.”

Fig. 2: EDA tools to help designers reuse IP need to account for area, thermal, PDN, and much more. Source: Qualcomm/DAC
The overall goal for engineers is to reduce runtime and compute, shortening time to market, increasing coverage and improving confidence at sign-off, and enabling engineers to be more productive. “We need innovation in GenAI, including GenAI that can create design input for the EDA tools, like a human designer, to drive fast convergence, and agents that can orchestrate design flows to reduce human effort for iteratively running tools to refine and optimize the design,” said Achour. “These are critical technologies to rapidly adapt common hardware to evolving AI product demand. We need innovation in AI for SoC design.”
Capturing IP data and design knowledge
Before AI can effectively help engineers adapt existing designs to new requirements, it needs access to accurate, organized information about the IP already available, including its configurations, constraints, dependencies, and previous implementations. Capturing and managing that information, along with the engineering knowledge and methodologies used to develop it, is essential to making AI-assisted derivative design scalable.
To help solve these challenges, established EDA vendors and startups are releasing physics-based, assistive AI co-pilot technology to speed up design exploration, PPA optimization, RTL generation, and verification.
However, before deploying an AI tool to create a brand-new design or a derivative design from existing IP, engineering teams must first collect the knowledge already inside the organization. After that, IP lifecycle management software is needed to connect engineering data, automate workflows, improve traceability, and make valuable IP easier to find and reuse.
“How do you pull different IPs, and where is information about that IP?” said Keysight’s Kamdar. “You could have information that says this IP works great for certain power levels. If you are developing an earbud, the available power may be much lower, so you know which IP will not be suitable. You have to look for a different source of IP from the finished product. You can create a software bill of materials (SBOM) or hardware bill of materials (HBOM) that lists all the IP you used, and you can confirm whether that was the latest and greatest version of the IP. Were there other variants of the IP? There are all kinds of different ways to do IP management.”
Teams also need a way to share the AI prompts, skills, and workflows they develop so that everyone can benefit from communal wisdom. “We invested in a platform and innovation store that allows our people to share prompts, plugins, check-ins, and solutions across teams,” said Ram Narayan, senior director of engineering at Arm. [2] “That was done primarily with the vision that teams can share skills and upskill themselves through that exchange. They can use the platform to upskill teams across the company, as well. This is an opportunity to bring people together around common ways of working and common learnings, which may have been lost over the years because we have acquisitions of groups, and groups going off and doing things differently. This is a real opportunity to enable these practices.”
An organization’s specific workflows need to be captured to get the best results from agentic AI-based design exploration tools.
“A company’s methodology is as important as the design, and the methodology they have used for the last 20 years to be able to tape out their chip has brought a lot of learning,” said Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at ChipAgents. “For example, ‘Use this cell/ don’t use this cell. Optimize for PPA that way. Don’t do this. Don’t do that. Or, do this.’ When you are in the ECO stage, and you have crosstalk, you can talk to the customer, and they say, ‘Oh, for crosstalk at this modem company, I have a very specific way of solving it. I have done the same thing for the last 10 years, and I am able to solve the crosstalk.’ That’s what we call the ontology.”
This is a very promising use case for agentic AI. A common approach from EDA tool providers today is to have an agentic collaboration platform sit with the customer, allowing sharing between users while also feeding data, methodology information, and design information back into agentic workflows so they can do the best possible job and deliver the best possible outcome. In ChipAgent’s approach, all proprietary customer data stays on-prem. “This belongs to the customer,” Rahim noted. “It is not something that comes back to us.”
Automating interconnect design
While organizations wrestle with how to apply AI, they also are leveraging improvements in algorithmic optimization, software-driven simulation, and deterministic EDA. This is especially important when it comes to data movement, which is one of the key performance bottlenecks, along with moving data in and out of memories and processors. A tiled, algorithmic fabric is easier to scale up or down for derivatives than crossbars.
“For our switch customers who have been working with crossbars in the past, and have had deep, lived experience over decades, it is still a very hands-on experience with hand-coding RTL to build huge custom networks, and almost hand-wiring things,” said Saurabh Gayen, chief solutions architect at Baya Systems. “They say, ‘When this wire comes in, it’s going to come in here, then this other data is going to come from there, and we’re going to make it like an arbiter. This is a painstaking process where the whole design just gets bigger and more difficult by an n-squared factor. This is super painful for engineers, companies, and project managers, as well. It’s an incredible source of risk for them, because it’s iterative. It’s manual. They don’t know if they’re going to find surprises later.”
Massive parallelism and other techniques have transformed what previously looked like a complex engineering project into a very manageable math problem. “Suddenly, this becomes an algorithmic construct that says mathematically we will give you the exact performance properties you need,” Gayen explained. “This will create, literally, a grid of identical tiles. Top-down, you get that guarantee that it meets the performance needs ahead of time. Then in terms of implementation, when it’s the physical design, you actually build it and harden those designs, then figure out how to put it within a chip.”
In today’s landscape, a software-first approach is needed to build hardware, adapt it to new use cases and better products, and reduce customer cost, pain, engineering effort, and time to tape out. “It’s all built step by step,” Gayen observed. “For example, when I came in, we already had a really good software-defined flow, which is new for hardware. People don’t like writing software. They like getting their hands dirty and writing RTL. Having that software perspective of coming in and generating RTL is something that unlocks a different type of thinking and allows breakthroughs like this to happen. Companies are happy, and the engineers are happy because they don’t have to do the painstaking manual work anymore.”
Multi-physics optimization limits
However, for design exploration or reusing IP, no tool yet optimizes timing, IR, and thermal together at the RTL or architecture level.
“Today, we don’t have anything that helps the RTL designer all the way,” said Vinay Patwardhan, senior director, product management at Cadence. [3] “We have something that can help customers from the netlist stage. We have a vision for going all the way to architectural, but right now it’s either timing-based improvement, IR-based improvement, or thermal-based improvement — not all three together as a multi-physics problem. If you want improvement at the RTL stage, you have to incorporate all of them into the source code, which isn’t available because thermal analysis works on layout layers. IR needs the locations of the power sources. At the RTL stage, there is no physical awareness of any of this, so it is a difficult problem. However, if we can find correct ways to model and abstract all those effects at that early stage, then it will be possible. There is some work going on in that phase, but to answer clearly, we don’t have anything in the RTL today. We can optimize the netlist continuously with feedback.”
Tool providers are addressing the challenge from many angles. For example, ChipAgents developed Build-A-Chip-Bench to evaluate AI agents from workload spec and RTL generation through synthesis, physical implementation, and layout verification.

Fig. 3: Key steps from workload specification to GDS. Dashed arrows show problems found downstream that send the agent back to revise an earlier step. Source: ChipAgents
While these advances show AI’s potential to automate increasingly complex design workflows, generating a design is only part of the challenge. Each stage of implementation introduces physical constraints and interdependencies that can affect decisions made earlier in the process. Changes intended to improve one aspect of a design may create problems elsewhere, requiring tools to account for the interactions among electrical, thermal, mechanical, and other physical effects.
The need for agentic tools to be grounded in fundamental physics is one reason why end-to-end solutions are still under development.
“The limiting problems are no longer inside the chip,” said Hardik Kabaria, CEO of Vinci. “They’re physical problems that live at the boundaries — heat moving from die to package to board to enclosure, thermo-mechanical stress across heterogeneous material stacks, power density interacting with cooling strategy at the system level. The physical world doesn’t respect the organizational boundaries the industry has drawn around it, and neither do the failures.”
Others agree. “EDA tools must expand beyond single-die optimization to system-level design, including multi-die integration, packaging, and software-hardware co-design, evolving toward intent-centric platforms rather than collections of disconnected point tools,” said Insaf Meliane, director of product management and marketing at Arteris. “One major gap is verification, where rising design complexity continues to outpace engineering productivity despite significant AI advances.”
These challenges become even more complex as designs move beyond the chip and package to the board level, where reused IP and previously verified components must operate within new electrical and physical environments. While reusing proven designs can reduce engineering effort, changes in placement, connectivity, and surrounding circuitry can introduce interactions that were not present in the original implementation. This makes verification a critical part of derivative design, even when the underlying components have already been validated.
Verification at the board level
As with SoC IP data management, a robust data management foundation enables teams to reuse known good blocks on the board.
“They verified them in the past, and they could say, ‘This block doesn’t need to be verified,'” said David Wiens, product marketing manager at Siemens EDA. “If they use that block more than once, they only need to verify it once. But in reality, blocks of data and blocks of designs can and will behave differently depending on what’s around them. It’s a step toward simpler verification, but you still have to be careful. You have this one circuit, and you place it on the top layer of the design, but whatever’s running underneath it that’s native to that, that’s custom to that design and may in fact interact with it. You could put a shield around it if you wanted to really trust it and really make sure that it’s not impacted. But particularly with signal integrity, that’s a bit of a scary proposition to say, ‘I’m just going to trust that it’s more than likely to pass by itself.’ It’s a question of what it interacts with on the board.”

Fig. 4: Data management is a key component of using AI tools to speed up any part of the design flow. Source: Siemens EDA
Agentic AI tools can now shrink verification time. Siemens reported that its HyperLynx Agentic Toolkit reduced the design analysis for 112 high-speed channels from several weeks to a couple hours. “In a manual process, engineers would first need to figure out the signaling protocol,” Wiens explained. “What SerDes protocol is it using? I’ve got to dig up the manual, which can be hundreds of pages long. I’ve got to find the rules within that, and the conditions to set up my simulator. Then I’ve got to push the button and wait for it, and then when I get it back, I’ve got to visualize. I’ve got to look at the results one waveform at a time. Did it pass? Did it fail? And if not, I’ve got to figure out why, and I’ve got to iterate.”
With new agentic solutions, the AI can inspect the database itself. “It can identify potential issues off the bat before it even simulates,” he said. “Then it automates the workflow. That’s a big thing because it’s part of what democratizes the tool. Specialists understand both the workflow and the results. Democratizing that automation, simplifying it, means anybody can push the button. With visualization, when you’ve got a ton of data, you don’t want to look at it one at a time. We can use AI to take that data and visualize it to produce different types of results that aren’t just simple waveforms. The AI can diagnose where the problem is. ‘This eye [diagram] is failing. Here’s where I think the problem is, and here’s what we recommend you do next.’ It takes the engineers through that entire path.”
The speedup doesn’t come only from AI and software capabilities. “It’s about leveraging hardware horsepower, GPU horsepower, CPU cluster horsepower,” said Wiens. “That’s what gets us the speed. But there are also areas of AI that help us explore the design space faster without brute-force simulation. Agentic AI accelerates the steps, mostly through smarter execution, and then delivers trusted outcomes because it’s physics-based. It’s leveraging known good simulation engines, and IP can be managed in a safe way on-prem.”
Leveraging GPUs and CPUs comes with computational costs, a concern raised by Qualcomm’s Achour. Moreover, engineers still must manually implement many of the changes recommended by agentic AI tools.
“What engineers do next is go back to the design, the actual layout or schematic, and make the changes that were recommended,” said Wiens. “Today, that’s still largely a manual process. Watch this space. Automating the actual place and route and things like that is a lot harder than automating workflow.”
What AI still can’t automate
AI-based design tools are advancing rapidly, with vendors introducing new capabilities for RTL generation, design exploration, physical optimization, and verification. These advances are reducing engineering effort in individual stages of the design process, but efficiently adapting existing hardware IP to new applications remains a much broader challenge.
Making derivative chip design more scalable will require more than increasingly capable AI models. Design teams need organized, accessible IP data; reusable engineering methodologies; tools that can evaluate architectural and physical trade-offs; and verification workflows that account for changes in configuration, implementation, and operating environment. Agentic AI may help connect and automate these processes, but the underlying tools must still produce results grounded in physical reality.
At the most fundamental level, many AI tools are text-based LLMs. “They are really, really good at predicting the next word, the next phrase, the next line, then the next paragraph, and that means AI can be used to write text-based chip design specs or chip design documents like RTL design,” said Keysight’s Kamdar. “AI can be used to write verification scripts that will test RTL and prove it’s good RTL or not, or find flaws in it. AI can read a long series of debug logs that could be gigabytes long, and humans will take forever to go through that. AI can quickly say, ‘Hey, did you go to line 79? That’s where I see a major issue.’ Largely, that’s what AI is helping with. There are so many other aspects of chip design that are not text-based, not suitable for words, and they still need humans actively.”
For chip architects and design teams, the opportunity is not simply to generate new designs faster, but to reduce the engineering effort required to turn proven IP into new products. Achieving that goal will depend on how effectively AI-driven automation can work with established EDA tools, engineering knowledge, and physics-based verification to identify what can be reused, determine what must change, and validate the resulting design. The real measure of AI’s success in derivative chip design will not be how quickly it generates new RTL, but how reliably it can help engineers transform existing IP into verified, physically viable designs with less manual effort.
